The Hefazat Ameer’s Criticism of Jamaat: Is the Style and Language He Uses a Reflection of His Personal Attitude, or of Hefazat’s Overall Character?

I frequently come across various strongly worded criticisms of Jamaat made by the respected Ameer of Hefazat on Facebook.

These remarks often provoke considerable debate between his supporters and critics, gradually giving rise to a sense of unease and undesirable tension.

Needless to say, as an individual, I have the right to criticise anyone—or any party, organisation, or ideology. If I find any of their ideas or positions unacceptable, the responsibility for my criticism naturally remains confined to my personal sphere.

If such criticism contains indecent language, distasteful expressions, or false information, it should be regarded as an expression of the individual’s lack of refinement, discourtesy, and transgression of proper limits.

Certainly, every party and organisation has some supporters or loyal groups who, in their reactions, pay little heed to etiquette or established norms. Even when their behaviour damages the reputation of the party or organisation, the organisations themselves are generally reluctant to accept responsibility for such conduct. On the contrary, they often seek to distance themselves from these activities and present themselves as entirely free of any association with them.

The situation, however, changes when I assume the position of a leader—an Ameer, head, or senior figure—of a party, organisation, or ideological group. At that point, I am no longer merely an individual; I become a symbol of an institution, an ideology, and a collective identity.

Consequently, the responsibility for any criticism I make extends beyond my personal sphere and also falls upon the party, organisation, or ideological group with which I am associated. My language, conduct, and manner of expression then become standards by which its leadership is judged.

If, as a leader, my language is refined, my manner is dignified, and my information is accurate, it enhances the reputation of my party and organisation.

Conversely, vulgar and discourteous language, coupled with baseless information, calls into question not only my own character but also the character of the organisation I represent.

This is because the character of the leadership is often reflected in the overall conduct of its followers. The familiar saying, **“الناس على دين ملوكهم”**—people follow the ways of their leaders—points precisely to this reality: the character of the leader influences the character and conduct of those who follow him.

Suppose a leader is courteous, restrained, and refined. His followers, as a whole, are likely to develop along similar lines and imbibe those values.

Conversely, if a leader is hot-tempered and abrasive in disposition, there is a strong possibility that similar traits will be reflected among his followers.

A beautiful couplet by a poet is particularly relevant here:

**“عَنِ المَرءِ لا تَسأَل وَسَل عَن قَرينَهُ، فَكُلُّ قَرينٍ بِالمُقارِنِ يَقتَدي”**

That is: *If you wish to know a person, do not ask about him; rather, look at his companion, for everyone tends to follow the example of those with whom they associate.*
